utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my native language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, and good morning to the Defence team. I'm here together with Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, co-counsel, as well as Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, we represent the Defence counsel of Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us is we have our legal assistant Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team, as well. Any preliminaries on your part, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. When it comes to filing yesterday -- sorry. Yes, Your Honour, I will repeat. When it comes to the filing of yesterday, with a view to the witnesses to add and not to call. In paragraph 7 of the referred motion, we named a person as a witness to add, which we didn't include in our witness list as such. So, and just a matter of being complete, we will file an addendum showing the complete witness list, including that name as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally on this motion, which I suppose you have received as well, I think I will be extremely brief and it's an invitation to the Defence rather than anything else. You know that we are doing our utmost to have the Prosecution rest its case by the end of May and not later. When I say "by the end of May, not later," plus/minus one or two days, all right. We would appreciate very much if, instead of taking the entire two weeks, 15 days, that you have according to the Rules to file your response, you try to file it earlier, possibly very early next -- this coming week. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have received the motion; we have reviewed it. It is also very important to us to have this trial completed, or rather the Prosecution case completed, as was envisaged; and in view of the cooperation we have had so far with the OTP, we will not object to these witnesses being placed on the list. Another matter that we have to review is the OTP's proposal regarding one of the witnesses, to have his supplemental statement read out. We will give a reply within two days regarding this; however, as for the other witnesses, we have no objections to them being placed on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And, Madam Vidovic, I must acknowledge, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, our appreciation for your cooperation. Yes, now this witness, I suppose you have got nothing to say before he comes in? I take it? No. How long do you expect -- who will be leading this witness. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I will be leading this witness, and I expect to be done with his examination-in-chief tomorrow. I do have a substantial amount of documents, exhibits, photographs, et cetera, that we would like to tender through this -- via this witness, and so I suspect that I will take at least one and a half sessions, if not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that leads us into tomorrow. And the Defence? Things being what they are and of course you haven't heard one single word coming out of this witness's mouth, I understand it will only be a rough guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we planned to complete the cross-examination of this witness in one day. However, the OTP delivered to us a vast number of documents, I think hundreds of documents, and a lot depends on how much time they will spend on the documents and how much time we will need to spend on them as well. So perhaps it might take as long as two days. We will do our best to complete it in one day though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you can't make an effort, Ms. Richardson, to finish this exercise in -- today?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is impossible, unfortunately. This witness is extremely important and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I know he is important, but I'm just trying to tap all the resources that I can think of. All right. Let's bring the witness in please. He doesn't enjoy any protective measures, does he?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, indeed, and he hasn't requested any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are a witness for the Prosecution in this case that has been instituted by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Mr. Naser Oric, and you will very soon start your testimony. Before you do so, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration in the sense or to the extent that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that Madam Usher is going to hand to you. Please read that text out loud, and that will be your commitment, your undertaking, with this Tribunal that you will be testifying the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. Yes. Welcome once more. As I said, you will start your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- your testimony in a matter of seconds. Of course most of us -- who will be cross-examining. Most of us, until we reach the cross-examination stage, will be speaking in English, so we have interpreters translating all the proceedings for you in your own language. It's important that you can follow the proceedings completely and that every single question and every single remark said here is translated into your language. If at any time there are problems with interpretation, or if at any time the volume is too loud or too low or you're not receiving interpretation at all, then please draw our attention straight away. Another thing that I wanted to tell you is that, you will be here for today and for tomorrow for sure, in all probability over the weekend. And then we will try and finish with you Monday, doing our best to finish by Monday. It's more or less a tiring exercise, sitting down and answering questions. I don't know if you have any court experience. If at any time you need a break, please let us know. We usually have a break every hour and a half and that there be a 25, 30-minute break. All right. Did I make myself well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Richardson from the Prosecution will be questioning you now, examining you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ibrahim Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And for the record, is it a fact that you are here testifying before this Tribunal by means of a subpoena, in that you are not voluntarily here of your own free will, but you are here to testify in this case because you were subpoenaed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please confirm the following information - if I misstate anything, please do correct me - you were born on July 18th, 1962; you were married; have two children; and you are of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You were born in the village of Opetci in the Srebrenica municipality and you lived in Srebrenica until 1995. You presently reside in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You are now a member -- presently a member of the federation army?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please tell us what position you hold there at this time and tell us when you were appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I am an officer for ethics in the human resources of the joint command of the federation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or rather the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was appointed to this position in September of last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how long have you held this position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: For about six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And prior to the present position that you presently fill, could you tell us what position you held and whether it was also a part of the Federation Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Starting with the creation of the joint command of the Federation Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1997, I was a member of the telecommunication administration of the joint command of the Federation Army. Starting in 1997 until 2004, I was in the telecommunications administration and served there as planning officer, officer for planning telecommunication links. My other position was an officer for management of units in the Federation Army, telecommunication units in the federation army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what period of time did you hold this position or these positions I should say?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: From July of 1997 until mid-2001, I was the planning officer in the telecommunications administration. And from mid-2001 until, July or rather September of 2004 I served as officer for management of organs and telecommunication units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And prior to 1997, were you employed and could you tell us with whom and what position, if any, did you have?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: From 1984, from December of 1984, I worked in the municipal centre for monitoring and alerting, therefore I was an operations officer in that centre for monitoring, informing, and alerting. I remained there until April of 2002 -- or rather until April of 1992, until the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Before we move to other positions, could you just tell us, very briefly, what were your duties during the time that you were employed from 1984 to 1992, with the municipal centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: My main tasks or main tasks of the persons serving as operations officers in the monitoring centre were to collect information from the field, or rather from the territory of the municipality pertaining to various emergencies and climate conditions, disasters, snowfalls and so on. This information was very important for the organs of Srebrenica, for the mayor who was to decide how to proceed in such cases. Based on information collected, the authorities decided in what area mechanisation ought to be used in order to clear away the snow, or in case where there were land-slides what steps ought to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in your capacity during the time that you held this position, did you receive any training or even prior to this position, were you trained in any particular skill?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1987, from September to December, I attended a training course for cryptographic encryption. In the former Yugoslavia, that was the highest training level for encryption tasks, for encrypting and decrypting written information. Upon completion of this course in December of 1997, or rather 1987, in addition to my previous duties, I was also authorised to conduct the tasks of encrypting and reading encrypted information. We had a service in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was organised in various regions. Srebrenica fell under the Tuzla region, as a result of which the information arriving from the republican executive council and sent to the municipal authorities went through these channels, which means that they were encrypted at the source side. And then that encrypted information was read at the final point and then made available to authorised officials. That means that if there was, for example, some information that originated from Srebrenica and was being sent to regional authorities, then that information was encrypted in Srebrenica and that the encrypted information was read in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Going back briefly to the position you held at the municipality. Did you have an opportunity to work with the local communities, in Srebrenica as well as Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica municipality -- rather, that territory was divided into 17 local communes. Majority of these local communes had communication links with the centre for monitoring, informing, and alerting. I will refer now to the centre as the centre for informing, just to make it easier, with your permission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. It is relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I have said go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you complete your answer, with respect to -- well, I will pose another question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said you were going to refer -- you asked for permission to refer to the centre as the centre for informing so that we could understand better, and I said "go ahead".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I collected information from the territory of local communes as well, because these were small territorial units within the municipality which did not have telephone links between each other. Therefore, the information that was needed, as I have explained to you earlier, was gathered via radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after you left the information -- your employment with the information centre, did you work anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Several days before the SDS of Srebrenica, or perhaps the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Yugoslav People's Army, or the volunteers perhaps, issued an ultimatum to the Muslims in Srebrenica to surrender their weapons, I worked in the centre for public security, or rather in MUP in Srebrenica, performing encrypting tasks there and forwarding this information to the regional centre in Tuzla or the Republican Ministry of the Interior in the Sarajevo. That was, therefore, several days before the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you completed your mandatory military service with the JNA. And could you tell us what year that was and whether or not you specialised in any particular fields or tasks.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I think on the 5th of July, 1982, until the 1st of August, 1983, so in that period of time I served my regular military service with the former Yugoslav People's Army. I performed my service in Kragujevac and in Rasko, which is in the territory of today's Serbia. Upon completing my military service I was trained and acquired skills in the signals field, communication field, and I specialised as an officer for radio telegraphing, which means that I was trained to use the Morse alphabet via radio links.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to draw your attention to Srebrenica and ask -- I would like to -- for you to tell the Trial Chamber what the ethnic makeup was of Srebrenica prior to the conflict in 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, in the territory of Srebrenica municipality there were about 37.000 inhabitants, about 72 or 73 per cent were Bosniaks Muslims, 25 per cent were Serbs, and the remaining 2 or 3 per cent were others, Yugoslavs, the Roma, Croats and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to Srebrenica, are you referring to Srebrenica the town, or is that number also encompassing other villages surrounding?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the entire territory of Srebrenica municipality. In other words, the town and the villages around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask the usher's assistance, I have a map that I would like the witness to take a look at. Please place this map on the ELMO and -- actually this portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The map is rather large so, Mr. Becirovic, you may have to manipulate it a bit. If you could take a look at the map that is presently on the ELMO, Mr. Becirovic, could you locate Srebrenica and, following that, could you locate the surrounding villages that make-up the municipality of Srebrenica. Maybe you can start out by circling Srebrenica on the map.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates] This part here, the encircled part, is the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness draws an oblong figure parallel to or perpendicular to Srebrenica on the map. Could you please put your initials next to that oval. Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you point or circle -- I know there are a number of villages, but circle the villages that are closest to Srebrenica that make up the municipality.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates] The village of Bajramovici, the village of Pusmulici. This stretch here, from Srebrenica to Bratunac, is mostly inhabited first of all there is the village of Gostilj. This is the village of Donji Potocari. There is no name, but that is what its name was. The village of Pecista, the village of Djogazi, the village of Gornji Potocari. Here there are a number of hamlets that make up the local commune of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me just stop you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. For the record, the witness has encircled all the places that he has just mentioned. Could you please put your initials against those circles, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You missed one, Mr. Becirovic, the unnamed one. The unnamed one just below Pecista.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: While you have the -- are those the major villages that make up Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: There are a number of other villages here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this. I think basically there should be agreement between Prosecution and Defence as to what constituted the municipality of Srebrenica, which towns, which villages. So if you are interested in identifying, on this map, particular villages, go ahead, put a direct -- a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then make a submission which the Defence can object to or dispute, whether -- if they don't agree that these form part of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I really need with respect to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: As you have the map before you, Mr. Becirovic, could you also point out for us where on the map Bratunac is located, the municipality of Bratunac. Please circle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. He doesn't need to point it out. We can see it, Ms. Richardson. Let's move. Let me just ask one question. You don't have reason to think that this map is not accurate, do you, Mr. Becirovic? This is an accurate map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any other questions with respect to the map at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, did there come a time when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Could the witness explain, what was the composition of the inhabitants in the town of Srebrenica. You have told us about the municipality. The town itself, the number of inhabitants there and how they were divided between Muslims and Serbs? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The town reflected the total composition of the population in the territory of the municipality. I don't have the exact data, but if there is a difference between the town of Srebrenica and the total area of the municipality of Srebrenica in that respect, it certainly isn't major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the population? I mean that's one other question that Judge Brydensholt asked you, the population of the town itself prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 3 and 4.000 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, we would ask that a number be given to this Prosecution's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be exhibit P521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Madam Registrar. This map will be admitted or is being admitted in evidence and is being marked as Prosecution Exhibit P521.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, did there come a time that tensions in Srebrenica, the Srebrenica municipality, rose between the ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This became noticeable as of September [as interpreted] 1992. Approximately, at the time when the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina expelled all non-Serbs from Bosanski Sabac also during the time of Arkan and Seselj's volunteers from Srebrenica were cleansing Bijeljina. During that time in Srebrenica, one could feel the pre-war psychosis, which resulted in the departure of a number of Serbs from Srebrenica - when I say "Serbs," I mean women, children, and the elderly - who moved towards Ljubovija and Bajina Basta in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a correction in the transcript. The witness mentioned February 1992 and here it says "September 1992." Can this be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thank Defence counsel. I noticed it myself and that was going to be my next question. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we agree, in fact, that that's what I thought I heard, too. So we're talking of February 1992 and not September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Becirovic it was in February of 1992 that you were just describing those events?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, February and March.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what, if anything else, of significance occurred during that month, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Due to the increased presence of Arkan's and Seselj's volunteers from Serbia, as well as of the reserve troops of the former JNA in Bratunac, Bosniaks experienced a great degree of fear, and together with their neighbours, Serbs, either at their own initiative or the initiative of the Serbs, attempted to keep guard in front of various buildings and facilities in order to feel safer there. And while the local politicians were trying to resolve the situation through frequent meetings of the National Council for Defence of Srebrenica, and they tried to convince the people that there was no reason for fear; however, these meetings were futile. A need arose at these meetings to talk about the administrative division of the municipality of Srebrenica. It was the Serbian Democratic Party of Srebrenica headed by Goran Zekic that insisted on that division? After a few meetings of that nature in April, Goran Zekic -- that the administrative division will not go through and the Serbian Democratic Party wanted to have control and power of the entire municipality of Srebrenica. And then the Srebrenica Muslims started leaving the town. They started departing for Tuzla, Slovenia, Germany, and some of the Muslims also found shelter in the villages around the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Had your answer been completed? My next question that I would ask you is: What occurred as a result of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, these meetings were being held, the Serbian Democratic Party armed the Serbs. There was a lot of propaganda activity. Information was being disseminated about Muslims being trained in the territory of Srebrenica. There was a lot of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what happened following these meetings and did there come a time that the population of Srebrenica, the Muslims, were advised of -- or were told -- I will rephrase the question. What happened following the meetings, with respect to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1992, information came from Bratunac, according to which a delegation of Muslims should go to Bratunac in order to agree on the way how life would proceed in Srebrenica. Sabit Begic, who was the director of the medical centre in Srebrenica; Cazim Salimovic, who had an administrative duty in the municipality of Srebrenica; and Salih Sehomerovic, who was a former mayor of Srebrenica and at the time he was retired; these three people went to that meeting. According to my information, at that meeting in Bratunac, they met with Arkan and some other men from his group who were wearing camouflaged uniforms with a Chetnik insignia. There was no conversation to speak of. There was also local politicians from the SDS of Bratunac. And at that meeting, the only thing that Arkan said was that on the 17th of April the Muslims of Bratunac should surrender their weapons; and he was referring to the active and reserve police forces as well as the -- those members of the Bosniak ethnicity who had hunting rifles. On the 18th of April, by 8 o'clock in the morning, the Muslims of Srebrenica were supposed to surrender their weapon; by the same token, they had to pledge loyalty to the Serbian government. On return of this delegation from Bratunac, Salih Sehomerovic went again either to Bratunac or Ljubovija where he had friends; I suppose he felt safer there. Sabit Begic and Cazim Salimovic left the town, went to -- in the direction of Tuzla or Sarajevo. I know that later on, in 1995, the both of them were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Bosniaks in Bratunac honoured the ultimatum; they surrendered their weapons. And only a few days later, the former JNA and the reserve forces and volunteers of Arkan and Seselj committed a slaughter in Glogova. They also expelled and slaughtered population in their local commune of Voljevica. Some of the population, the women and the children, on the 10th May, about 10.000 people were deported to Bratunac. And in Bratunac itself, in the primary school called Vuk Karadzic they executed in a most beastly way about 2 -- 2.500 men, mostly educated people? In that group was also Sali Sehomerovic, he was also killed. That's the person who was a member of that delegation I was talking about. The Bosniaks of Srebrenica did not surrender their weapons. They mostly left the town. One group rallied around Naser Oric in Potocari. Another group rallied around Hakija Meholjic in the Stari Grad sector; one group rallied around Akif Ustic and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think rather than say "and so on and so forth," let's finish the list. Akif Ustic, where did people -- in which particular area did people rally around Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also in the Stari Grad sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is that all? Is it just Akif Ustic, Meholjic, and Oric, or was there rallying by people around someone else as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April 1992, that was all. Later on as of the beginning of May, there were other groups in other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the territory of Suceska, they rallied around Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else that you remember? That you can remember? I'm trying to chase this up --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- because I realise that this witness, if you let him speak, I think we will get most information out without a long series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were any other areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now we have Tursunovic, Oric, Meholjic, and Akic -- Akif Ustic. Anyone else in particular that you can remember? We are in May now of 1992, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the individuals that you just named for the Court, could you tell us whether or not you were familiar with any of these individuals prior to May of 1992. Let's first start with Mr. Naser Oric; did you know him before? And could you tell us what, if anything, did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Naser Oric directly. I was familiar with a face. I saw him in town immediately prior to April 1992. I found him interesting, because up to then he worked in Belgrade for a number of years. He was a personal guard to Slobodan Milosevic. And I lived in a small town, and I found such a person interesting, without any particular reason. He was young, he was handsome, athletically built. And I believe that he might have been a good person to socialise with, although I was not among those who socialised with him. I knew Zulfo Tursunovic well, because I am native -- a native of the same local commune that he was a native of. He was a farmer. And that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is there anything else in particular with respect to Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic, other than being a farmer, that you knew about him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this Trial Chamber will find it interesting to know that before the war, Zulfo had a murder case pinned to him and I believe that he spent some 14 years in prison. This is something that may be should be said about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And I would just like to go back for a moment, briefly, to Naser Oric. Where did he live prior to -- where was he from, what area of Srebrenica, and what role did he play, prior to the -- you described for us previously as people rallying around him? Did he have a particular position in Potocari -- excuse me, in the area he was from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was born in Gornji Potocari; that's where his parents lived. And prior to April 1992, he was the commander of the forward command post of the public security station of Srebrenica, that was located in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How did you know Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: From the December, and I knew Hakija as a policeman. And in 1992, Hakija was already retired; he lived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And that's Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Akif Ustic, I didn't know him before. He was a teacher who worked in the primary school of Srebrenica. I met him for the first time in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you left Srebrenica in or around the time of April 1992? And could you tell us, very briefly, where you went and -- well, that's it for now.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, 1992, I left Srebrenica and I went via Potocari and Buljim mountain to my place of birth in the local commune of Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And briefly tell us what you did in Suceska and how long you stayed there.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of April when I arrived in Suceska, the war was less present in the air, if I can say so. People still continued working in the bauxite mine, for example. I expected that the war would be over soon and that I would be able to return back to my job in Srebrenica. However, that did not happen. On the 1st of May or perhaps the 2nd of May, 1992, an incident occurred. A group of Muslims who worked in the bauxite mine in Milici, where the reserve forces of the JNA were being trained, were called to come in and receive their monthly salaries. Serbs, on that day, detained about 30 Muslims from Suceska and Derventa. Derventa is in Vlasenica municipality, however it is closely linked with local commune Suceska local commune. They sent an ultimatum via one of the workers for the Muslims in Suceska to surrender their weapons or else Suceska would be burned down. On the following day, an attack ensued, launched from Milici against Suceska local commune. They came to Zutica with four APCs or perhaps four tanks. Since this was in the afternoon, the attack was stopped and the Serbs burned Homalja [phoen] village and Olavaca [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- upon which the Serbs retreated. When they burned down villages, they also detained women and children, took them to the camp in Milici, and the men fit for military service fled to the forests. On the following day they continued with burning villages, Basta, Nurici, Stedra, Stedric, Dzile.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you for a moment. Before we talk about the events -- well, let's just go back for a moment, I should say. Why was it that you left Srebrenica in April?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I was afraid. I didn't feel safe, since all of the Muslims had already left the town. On the 18th of April, when the ultimatum expired at 10.00 to surrender weapons and the weapons had not been surrendered, the Serbs started shelling, first in the area of Budak village and then Donji Potocari. Later on, on the 19th and 20th of April, they shelled with mortars, Gornji Potocari, Donji Potocari, and so on. People fled with their bare -- basic belongings in any direction they could. The road between Bratunac and Srebrenica was also shelled. People were hoping that to would be over soon and that they would be able to return soon. A man was killed on the 18th of April in Gornji Potocari by a shrapnel. On the 19th, I decided to leave the area and go to my birthplace.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were your wife and children still in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I sent my wife and my child, I think on the 12th of April, with a convoy, the Red Cross convoy, away. First they went to the refugee centre in Rijeka in Croatia; and later on, they spent the rest of the war in Ljublijana, in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you returned to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, before the shelling started and before the ultimatum expired, I returned to the police station in Srebrenica with another man. The situation, the atmosphere, in this city was terrible. There were no people in the street. There was snow falling. The police station was deserted. There were -- therefore, there was nobody there. We established contact with Avdo Hebib, who at the time was in the republican MUP. We informed him of the situation. We told him what they atmosphere was like, asked him what to do; he suggested that we should leave town as well, not dwell there any longer. At around 10.00, before the shelling started, we arrived in Gornji Potocari. That was my first encounter with shells, with explosion of shells. On the 18th of April, we attempted to leave town. We arrived in Vidikovac, which is a suburb and where a neighbour of mine was who called, via the telephone, the police station, as he wanted to check what was going on. The person on the other side of the line who picked up the phone was Ostoja Bozic, who before the war was a reserve policeman in the Srebrenica police station. He told him that the Serb authorities were in place, that they had been established, that the Serb authorities placed their people in the Srebrenica police station. He offered him to express his loyalty. Sidik used to be a policeman before the war as well; however, we did not dare go back. On that day, before the Vidikovac settlement we came across a barricade, a patrol, with two people wearing camouflage uniforms, green-olive, with weapons who most likely were members of the Serb Territorial Defence. They stopped us, asked us where we were headed; we explained that Sidik wanted to go to his house. On our way back, they didn't stop us, they let us through, and we went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you to go forward a little bit to when you return to Srebrenica after leaving and being in Suceska. What state -- when did you return to Srebrenica and, could you tell the Trial Chamber what state you found the town in when you returned.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Around the 20th of May, 1992, I returned from Suceska to Srebrenica. The town was deserted. The Serbs had already left the town. Some of the Muslim residents, who just prior to Arkan's and Seselj's people left -- had left the area, started coming back were there. The town was partially looted. All of the vehicles that had been left by Muslims there were transported mostly to Serbia. Everything that they could take with them, household appliances, TV sets, and all other valuable technical goods were looted. The shops were demolished. Many Muslim apartments were looted?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you speak with anyone?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I met Akif Ustic then in a suburb called Kazani. We spent a brief period of time together. There was some other people there with us. We discussed what had happened. I asked him whether the centre for informing, where I used to work, was looted and whether the communications equipment was still there; he didn't know and told me that I should go and look myself. On that day, I returned to Suceska once again and, after several days, went back to Srebrenica, visited the premises of the centre for informing, saw that it had not been broken into. This was located behind the municipal building in Srebrenica. I did not have the keys then, and later on we were given the keys. We entered the premises and found the equipment there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Before we get to the equipment that you found, did he tell you anything else with respect to what had happened in the town during the time that you were absent?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: It is well-known that on the 8th of May, 1992, Goran Zekic was killed; he was ambushed. On the 9th of May -- rather on the 8th, in the evening and on the 9th of May, the Serbs left the town. Akif Ustic was in the Stari Grad sector. He told us that there was no major fighting there, that there was only sporadic exchange of fire between his group and the Chetniks. He mentioned that three members of the white eagles, I think, were killed in that sector, between the Stari Grad and the town. He also said that one of his relatives had been killed. So, there was no intense fighting there, and the Serbs left the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the neighbouring villages and the people that you mentioned, which is Naser Oric and Hakija Meholjic, could you tell us whether or not Akif Ustic told you what happened with respect to them.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What happened to whom, to Akif.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will repeat the -- I will repeat my question and make it a little bit more clear. With respect to Naser Oric, for instance, did Akif tell you what happened with Naser Oric and the people who had rallied around him, or rallied around Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to Hakija Meholjic, did he say anything with respect to Hakija and the men that Hakija had rallied around him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Since Hakija Meholjic and his people were in the forest, near the area where Akif Ustic was, when he spoke about sporadic shooting and exchange of fire between the Serbs and his group, he wasn't sure whether Hakija and his group took part in it as well. So he didn't really say anything special about Hakija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to Hakija and his group, who were the men that made up the group that Hakija had with him, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Those were mostly members of police force, both the active police force and the reserve police force from Srebrenica who, on the 17th, the night between the 17th and the 18th, wanted to go with Hakija. There were some who didn't with a to go with Hakija and went to neighbouring villages. At the time, I did not know these people, none except Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you arrived at the communication building, could you tell us what the condition of the building was and whether you found any equipment there.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in the building of the centre for informing, I saw that the front door was locked. At the time, we couldn't enter the premises. I knew that a certain Bekir Salihovic, who used to work in the centre for informing before the war, possibly had the key; that was my assumption. I wanted to find him and find the key so that we wouldn't have to break down the door. After several days Bekir Salihovic brought the key; this took some seven to ten days perhaps, because he wasn't in town at the time. So we opened the door, entered the premises of the centre for informing, found the equipment there, several radio stations, radios, which were used before the war by the centre for monitoring, informing, and alerting. Therefore, the equipment was in tact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber exactly what equipment you found, the names of the equipment and the type of equipment that you found.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In the centre for informing, there was a radio manufactured by Iskra before the war, the factory in Slovenia called Iskra. This was used to establish radio connection with local communes. In addition to that, there was a radio device of Japanese origin, IC-345 [as interpreted]. Before the war, it was owned by the Srebrenica radio club, and via this device, the ham operators from Srebrenica contacted ham Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. operators throughout the world. In addition to this, there were another two radio devices, Atlas 220-X, which were owned by the centre for informing before the war. They were not used before the war and the idea was to use them in case of exercises, or some training purposes. They were compatible with the radio device ICN-45 [as interpreted]. These are older types of equipment, dating back to the Second World War, the American type of equipment, and at that period of time they were not really useful. In addition to that, there were another two small radio devices owned by civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness is discussing the types of equipment and I think it is very important, in two instances, when he said "IC" he said "745," and in both instances this was incorrectly recorded. And I believe that it is very important to have accurate information regarding the exact type of equipment used, and I hope that this can be corrected in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as I may, I agree with the Defence and I noticed it myself and was about to go over that again. So maybe we can ask the witness to clarify and have another answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. When you referred to this radio device, I think it's of Japanese origin, IC, is it IC-745?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us how many of that type of equipment, the IC-745, you found in the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. At this stage perhaps you can ask the witness, because we will need the information in any case, the size of this equipment, these various radio devices that he saw there, what were their size? Can we go through them one by one, please. Let's start with this Japanese IC-745. How big was it and where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the offices where the centre for informing was headquartered, there was one room used by the Srebrenica radio club before the war, and it was in that room that the IC-745 device was located. Its dimensions, approximate dimensions, are as follows: 35 to 40 centimetres in width; the length, perhaps 40 centimetres also; and its height was perhaps 15 centimetres. On the front panel, there were various buttons which could be used to change frequency, working frequency, then there was the antenna tuner, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time, if I may, to have the -- I apologise. Perhaps this is a good time, if I may, to have the witness look at an exhibit of the radio he's describing and we do have copies, and this is also in Sanction I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There is an additional copy, if the usher could take it from me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, you can see on your screen a photo of -- or two photos of what appear to be radio transmitter receivers. Could you help us identify either or both of them, please. The one on the top, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is IC-745 piece of equipment, which I found in the premises of the radio club, or rather the premises of the centre for informing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the one below it, underneath it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one underneath is IC-751, also manufactured in Japan of a somewhat newer production and of a better quality when it comes to tuning the antenna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was there an IC-751 on the premises that you visited on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson. Shall we give this document a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 522, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 522. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just to complete the picture of the IC-745, Mr. Becirovic, could you tell us from looking at this photograph what is not -- what is not present? In other words, is there a microphone or are there headphones? Are there any other piece of attachments to this radio that we don't see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it important, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. That's -- if it is important, let's go to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question is specifically with respect to -- excuse me, if I may, so that we're clear. We're talking about the equipment that you found in the information centre. And could you tell us, based on this photograph, if there is something else that is a part of this equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The set also contained the transformer from 220, to 212 [as interpreted] volts; in addition to this, there were headphones and a microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I have one exhibit with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it 204 -- 240 to 212? 220 to 212? There seems to be something wrong there. The transformer would lower the voltage from 240 to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 220 to 12 volts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To 12 volts, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I think this is a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, before the break, you were describing for us the 745 -- the IC-745; you said it was made by the Japanese I believe. Could you tell us whether this piece of equipment was operational when you found it in the information centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was operational?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber how this piece of equipment works and describe for us the system, the manner in which it is used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Briefly. I mean, we don't need a whole technical explanation. Just briefly explain the use, normal use, of this set and how it's -- while operated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have already said that it is an amateur piece of equipment and radio amateurs were people who were volunteers, who joined the organisation in order to make contact with somebody all over the world. It's very simple to use. You press on the microphone button, and you could talk into the microphone. And all those who were on the frequency that was predetermined, could hear you when you did that. The conversations were mostly very short. It is a common practice, due to the fact that this is a very sensitive type of equipment; and after longer broadcast, it would break down. That's why these transmissions were, for the most part, very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "very brief", could you give us an idea in minutes, five minutes, ten minutes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Two minutes at the most. Most often this was under a minute, because the messages were really brief. You just transmitted the code, and you provide the other participant in the conversation to give you their code signal. Then you give your name, your first name, your last name, or the place from which you are transmitting. You offer the other participant the same possibility to do the same, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say a "brief conversation," do you mean -- if you could just explain further, by the minute you mean per -- every time you spoke to someone you would only speak for a minute? Or that was the entire time that you could speak for, the conversation would last only a minute?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: No, you did not understand me properly. One participant could just engage in a very short exchange and then provided the other participant to do the same. The entire conversation could well take over an hour if that was the case, but one exchange was very short.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And -- pardon me, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: For example, when there were competitions of ham operators before the war, it would happen that there were over 20 participants in one conversation. So that when each of these participants had to be given an opportunity to introduce themselves to say where they were transmitting from, that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. For the record, I noticed that Mr. Wubben and Mr. Di Fazio are no longer present in the courtroom and that Ms. Patricia Sellers is present instead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the conversation, would this conversation be in code or just conversation in an ordinary language?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Those were open conversations; there was no coding involved. It was just a normal conversation, as if people were in one room, facing each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, you said that this IC-745 enabled you to reach anyone all over the world. Now, does that include, just for the record, the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Zagreb, Croatia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, at around the time you found this equipment, I believe you said it was May of 1992 - please correct me if I'm wrong - how many radios, such as the IC-745, were in the possession of people in the local communities surrounding Srebrenica or Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: The radio sets such as IC-745 did not exist in any of the local communes. Towards the end of May 1992 I found this radio set. I've already said that in the local communes there were the so-called Iskra radio sets, I-s-k-r-a, which had only one frequency. Their frequency was determined by means of crystals and it could not be altered in any way. So these conversations could take place only between the people who were in possession of that particular type of equipment; there could not be exchanges between different types of equipment involving that particular one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the other equipment that you found, you just mentioned Iskra, and could you tell us whether or not this Iskra, how many of those you recovered in the information building and whether they were in -- they were in working condition, operational?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: There was one such equipment and it was operational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How big was it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The front panel was somewhat thinner than IC-745; it was about 10 centimetres. It was somewhat shorter, and it was about 35 to 40 centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You testified that there were 17 local stations in the community and they all had the Iskra. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: 17 local communes there were, that is correct. And those local communes that had telephone lines, they did not have ham radios, for example Skelani, the local community of Sase, for example. And the others did have the same type of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it there were people in the local communities who had the capacity to operate these radios?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those ham radios could usually be found in the offices of the local communes. That's when the newborn babies used to be registered, the marriages were registered, and those offices were integral parts of the administrative services. There were registrars who worked in those offices, and they could also operate those ham radios. And it was easy to operate a ham radio once it was installed, and it just was a matter of somebody pressing the microphone button and starting talking into the microphone. Those ham radios required 220 volt power.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit about the Atlas radio that you mentioned earlier. Did you also find one of those, and could you tell us whether or not it was in working condition, and, as Your Honour asked before, could you describe the size, give us a description of it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Atlas 210-X was operational; it was somewhat bigger than the IC-745. As far as I can remember, the front panel was about 20 centimetres high. It was about 60 centimetres wide, and in depth its length was about 35 to 40 centimetres. I've already said that this is a somewhat older piece of equipment and it mostly operated on the principle of transistors and the -- it was not as good as the IC-745 in terms of reception.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many of those did you recover in the information centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please tell us whether or not you recovered any other type of communication equipment or apparatus or materials.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, there were three pieces of equipment, somewhat smaller, that used to be used by the civilian protection before the war. Their range was very short, maybe 3 to 5 kilometres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were these operational?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were operational. They were of somewhat older make. The weight was about 3 to 4 kilogrammes, so they were easily transported.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Where did you -- anything else, any other type of communication materials, not necessarily equipment, but any other type of materials?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the premises of the information centre before the war, there was one part where there was a storage of the civilian protection; there you could find the fire extinguishers. There was also a terminal from which alerts were sounded before the war, in case of fires and similar things. And Alerts were given for some other types of danger as well. In the town itself, there were two alert sirens, and from that terminal both of these sirens could be activated at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you find any material such as any materials relating to codes or code documents at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was also the piece of equipment called KZV-41 [as interpreted], which was intended for coding and decoding of written information. There was also -- there were teleprinter pieces; one were together with the KZV-41 [as interpreted] for coding and decoding. And the other printer, before the war, was used for the transmission of coded information to Tuzla, mostly in Tuzla. It had to use a telephone line, and that's how we could communicate before the war and this was done once or twice a day or when the need for that arose.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it was KZU, not KZV.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the telephone lines, in May of 1992 when you -- at around the time you found this equipment in Srebrenica, were the telephones working?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were working for a period of time after May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was there electricity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In May and up to mid-June there was electricity, and after that the whole territory of Srebrenica municipality was cut off by the Serbs. The Serbs cut off the electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I would like to bring you back to the day that you found the telephone equipment -- the communication equipment that you just testified to. What did you do with the equipment? In other words -- I should rephrase the question? What, if anything, did you do after you found the equipment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: For a while I tried to listen in and hear whatever I could hear on those frequencies. I did that in coordination with Akif Ustic. And I believe that on several occasions I heard about the activities of the Serbian forces around Visegrad, Gorazde, Foca, and areas in between those places. In more specific terms, on one morning I heard about the preparations for an attack on Kopacevo [as interpreted], a village near Gorazde. I found it very strange to hear that an attack order was being transmitted in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Before we talk about what you overheard -- what you heard on the radio, excuse me, could you tell us about the conversation with Akif and when did this conversation take place. And tell us -- tell us what the contents of the conversation included, consisted of.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: The first contact I had with Akif took place around 29th of May, 1992, in Kazani. That is when we spoke about the premises of the information centre, when I wanted to know whether they had ever been broken in. When I returned from Suceska and when I entered those premises and when I learned what the equipment was available to me, there Akif asked me to listen in and see whether I could hear any information about the Chetnik attacks and where they were taking place. And as a result of that, I could hear what I mentioned a little while ago. Some ten days later, after I started listening in, I got in touch with ham operators from the Tuzla region. Up to the 10th of May, 1992, after having executed the large group in the primary school, the Serbs deported some 10.000 of women, children, elderly from the area of Bratunac towards the region of Tuzla. Some of the male population stayed behind and after that expulsion moved to the territory not under the control of Serbs. And a need arose to connect the parts of the families which were in different parts of the territory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment, Mr. Becirovic. We will get to that with respect to what happened in Bratunac in a moment. But just going back to the conversation you had with Akif, he told you to listen. Did he tell you -- how often did you listen? Did you listen every day? And could you tell us, what piece of equipment you used to listen in.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: At that time there was electricity. I could spend as long as ten hours by the equipment and I could listen in. I used the IC-741 [as interpreted] to listen in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 745, the interpret's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not easy for me to do, because during the 10 or 12 hours I could only hear short periods of 10 or 15 minutes that I found useful. And that's why after 10 days, I told Akif that it was not really very practical, that the information that I could hear could not be used in Srebrenica, that we did not have any means of conveying that information to the areas where the attacks were supposed to take place. And in the meantime the different need arose, and that's why I suggested that maybe it would be better for us to try and learn how many people from the area of Bratunac had been deported to Tuzla, how many of them could still be found in Tuzla, and to try and obtain information about their members of family who had remained in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, I am not really familiar with this piece of equipment, the IC-745, although I am familiar with others. But when -- during this exercise that you are mentioning to us, does the IC-745 operate also as a scanner automatically? Does it scan for frequencies that are being used at any given time, or do you have to search for them manually? Just by chance, you keep doing a manual scan yourself until you hit on something? How did it work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had to do it manually. I had to turn a button that changed my frequencies for me. And at the moment when I heard somebody on a particular frequency, I would stop and I would listen in for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thought so much, but of course that becomes an extremely tiring and boring exercise. Those of us who say -- know well enough about it, yes. Let's go, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, were you able to, if you wanted to, speak with someone on the other side who had this similar type of equipment, the 745?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The information you heard, it was with respect to military actions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, there was the mention of an artillery attack on the village of Kopacevo, after which an infantry attack would follow. I heard somebody, I don't know who it was, issuing an order for the village of Kopacevo to be shelled for an hour, and after that and infantry attack was ordered. And this order was being conveyed and transmitted for maybe a minute or so. And after that, I didn't hear anything about the -- that attack and how it developed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many such communication regarding -- how many such discussions about military actions did you overhear, and were these actions -- who were you listening to? Could you tell us if it was Serbs, Muslims or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to this attack on the village of Kopaci, I remember maybe one or two similar attacks, also in the area of Visegrad, the municipality of Visegrad, Gorazde, and Foca. Immediately after that, maybe a day after that, I could see on my topographic map the places that were mentioned and I could locate the places where these attacks were taking place. I would normally hear the details of attacks undertaken by the Serbian forces against Muslims in the areas of Gorazde, Visegrad, and Foca. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you received this information, you report it -- to whom did you report it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I just made a brief note of what I had heard. I would mention the names of the villages that were mentioned, without any detailed explanations, because I was not aware of any details. And I would take those notes to Akif Ustic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How often did you take the notes to Akif and what period of time was this? By that I mean the month.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: That was in late May and early June 1992, and it happened maybe three or four times. When I had information -- when I didn't have any information, there was nothing for me to take to Akif.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The information that you heard, did you later learn -- I will rephrase the question. Was the information that you heard accurate? Did you later learn that these attacks in fact did take place?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could listen to the radio Sarajevo station, which was the radio of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on those same days or one or two days later, when the media were informed of those attacks, they would broadcast information about those attacks that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you give the information to anyone other than Akif, and could you tell us what, if anything, he did with the information you gave him, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not provide anybody else with that information, save for Akif Ustic. It was my impression that Akif didn't know himself how to make this information useful, and that's why this activity was short lived and I opted for the other type of activity. And Akif agreed with me that I should try and obtain information on the Muslims who had been deported from Bratunac and providing that information to their family members in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Specifically did Akif tell you whether or not he had passed the information on to someone, or you just assumed he did not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: He never told me that he passed this information on to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And please tell the Trial Chamber why you decided to take the information to Akif, as opposed to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, simply speaking, Akif was a person around whom a group of Bosniaks rallied, Bosniaks who were there in town. I did not hear from anybody else, nor did anybody else tell me to take this information to anybody else. We had an arrangement with Akif to take information to him. At the time, I did not -- I did not believe this to be a duty of mine, to provide this information, nor would I take this information to anybody else, had I been requested to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson. Apart from Akif Ustic, was there anyone else who was aware of what you were doing at the time, in other words, that you were listening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, after you suspended your reporting to Akif, this information --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My learned friend earlier used the phrase "reporting" as if there was some reporting obligation, and the witness referred to taking notes. He has since clarified there was no duty, so I would object to characterising this as reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: After you suspended your activities of passing this information on to Akif, what, if anything, did you do after this? You said, previously, that you -- that there was a suggestion to contact families. Could you tell us a little bit more about that, and how did you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time in the city of Srebrenica, I would come across many people who had been forced out of Voljevica or from parts of Bratunac municipalities, which had been occupied by Serb forces. Their families had been deported to the Tuzla region or perhaps elsewhere, Croatia, Germany. Since the radio station was an only possibility to hear some information from Tuzla, Srebrenica, or elsewhere - and again to pass information on from Srebrenica - it occurred to me that this would be a way of helping these people so that they can find information about the whereabouts of their family members. This is how I got in contact with ham radio operators from Tuzla region, first of all the club called BMN, in Tuzla, the radio club where a certain lady called Nada worked. When we first met, I asked her whether there were any people from Bratunac in Tuzla, people who had been deported from Bratunac; and she told me that she had heard that there were some people registered by the local Red Cross. I asked her whether she could get the lists of these persons with their addresses, which she accepted to do. And in a way she alerted, or rather got into contact with other radio clubs, Zivinice, Banovici, Srebrenik - all of these locations are in Tuzla municipality - and she asked them to do the same activity in their places, to gather lists of persons who had been deported from Bratunac and to pass it on to me in Srebrenica. We did this for the following two or three months perhaps, and naturally, this could not have been accomplished in one day. I would normally receive 20 names per day, sometimes more. So in the following two or three months, we collected the names of all refugees from the Bratunac municipality who were in the Tuzla region. Upon receiving these lists, after Nada in Tuzla would read it out to me, into mike, I would write it down, and this was a very slow process. And then I would put these lists with names on the board in the place where I was. Very often, when family members in Srebrenica asked me something, I would explain it to them directly, about the information I received, about the accommodation that these people had in the Tuzla region, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, did you advise Akif that you had contacted Nada?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told him immediately upon establishing contact with her, and I explained to him what we could do with this, that this was a way of compiling lists of people deported from Bratunac. I said that this would be a way to help families whose members were in Srebrenica and in the Tuzla region, that they could acquire information about their close ones and their whereabouts. In addition to that, I also had occasion to pass on tragic news to people. Sometimes during deportation process there were victims, people were killed.
