So I could pass information about people killed in Bratunac, in the Vuk Karadzic school or in the shelling, in the forest. I realised that there was no purpose in hiding the truth, that no purpose was served by that, and that this information should be conveyed to the families in Tuzla and that somebody should inform them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The system that you had with respect to contacting the families, I would like you to concentrate on the month of June 1992. Could you tell us whether or not people were permitted to come to the information centre and actually speak on the radio to the family members, or were you simply taking messages and relaying them to the family members?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In June of 1992, it was not permitted. People didn't even know that that could be done. Very few people knew how to use this equipment. Therefore, they were quite happy to receive first-hand information about their family members being safe. They did not even insist on this, because very -- a lot of them didn't even know that it was possible to establish contact in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many operators -- I will rephrase the question? Were you the only person operating the radio at this time at the information centre?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In June, a young man arrived who used to be a ham radio operator before the war, Abid Zukic. He had a secondary school education. He helped me a great deal in collecting this information, because this was quite a large task, writing down these lists. Except for the two of us, nobody else performed this type of work in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: On a daily basis, could you tell us how many hours you worked and how many messages you sent and how many you received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, I hate to interrupt, but we've been spending the last 45 minutes, approximately, on this. What's the relevance of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe that the relevance is the capacity during that period of time to -- for information to come into Srebrenica as well as to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But don't you think that we've heard enough on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you think that it's appropriate at this time to end this line, I will oblige.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 45 minutes on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's not a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I am -- as we go along, I'm gathering the -- forming the impression that we are nowhere, nowhere coming to an end of the examination-in-chief by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I should say with respect to the number of exhibits that I intended to use, I will not use as many as I proposed. It was sort of an abundance of caution, and I have since then taken another approach and I will probably use half so -- but again, if you think this is a good time to end this line, I can do that. If you've heard enough, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day, what we are interested in is whether this equipment or any other equipment that he knows of or he could tell us about was available and made use of during the conflict for purposes that are relevant to our case. The rest, I mean about these refugees and-- we are not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at least in my mind anyway, I thought it was relevant with respect to the capacity and the ability --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we could have handled that with one direct question: What was the capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Nada and BMN, were you able to contact any other operators during the month of June in Tuzla? Were you able to contact operators outside of Tuzla and any other place.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I contacted operators in Zivinice, Banovici, Lukavac, Gracanica, Srebrenik, Lipnica municipalities, mostly these places, because it was in those areas that refugees from Bratunac were housed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, what -- could you tell us what happened the following month. You -- I take it you undertook this for most of June, is that so?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This work was continued in July. I told you, two or three months. However, in July I found another piece of equipment in the police station. Initially it wasn't operational, however we repaired it. When I found it, it did not have a microphone. Once we found the microphone, I installed it, it became operational, and then I moved that piece of equipment to the post office in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So one question. We are in June now and even later than June. When -- according to your testimony, before the electricity supply had practically ceased in Srebrenica, how were you able to operate these transmitters-receivers without electricity? Because I take it that even the transformer would need electricity in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I mentioned earlier that the power was cut off, I apologise. I think that I simply said "until the power was cut off." I did not give a particular period of time. I think that the power was cut off in July, and until early July, we were able to use electrical current, 220 volts. After that, once the power was cut off, we were forced to use either batteries from cars or some other types of batteries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- using the DC current.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: While we're on the topic of electricity, maybe we can stay there for a moment. When the power was cut off in July, could you just explain to us the system -- any systems that existed after that period of time where you were able to get electricity and also how you were able to operate the radios.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In the post office building, there was a room where, before the war, there were batteries, and this was used for the automatic telephone exchange for Srebrenica in case there were any power outages. Initially, I used these batteries to supply current to the equipment that I used. In addition to that, we had a small generator, which was used for a piece of equipment in a hospital, used to sterilise medical equipment. By way -- we used that generator as long as we had oil to use it -- to run it. After that, we planned to build a small, mini, power station. Perhaps it's difficult to understand it all now, but it occurred to us that we could use a 5 kilowatt machine and to put it in, plug it in, and connect it with a water supply so that we could produce, I think not more than 3 kilowatt power, which was quite unstable in supply. And this mini power plant was initially used just to provide light in the hospital and to operate the autoclave, the sterilising equipment. However, as I said, this was quite an unstable source of power. And later on, we used this power source to recharge the batteries, which, in turn, were used to run radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to the power, the makeshift power apparatus that had been constructed, do you know if any other individuals in Srebrenica were able to do the same to -- so that they could have some electricity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This took place after the demilitarisation. In Srebrenica, there were perhaps five, six, or seven such mini power plants at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Are we interested in what happened after the demilitarisation, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask another question, after that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then finish. So this happened after the demilitarisation, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour. I would like the witness to be shown an exhibit at this time. And if we could -- if the witness could also be shown the prior exhibit, which has this -- the IC-745 on it, Prosecution's Exhibit 522.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem? Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you a question prior to your -- discussing the exhibit before you. You said in the second half of June you went to the police station. Is that correct? And could you tell us if you recovered any communication equipment in that police station.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already explained that I found this piece of radio equipment IC-751 at the police station. It lacked a microphone. Everything was in disorder in those premises. A few days later I found a microphone and this radio set was operational, and I could install the microphone in. Therefore, in early July, via IC-751, I established communication from the post office building, with the ham operators in Tuzla, whereby we started collecting information on the deported civilians from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after you relocated this piece of equipment, what, if anything, happened after that? Did anyone operate this equipment, piece of equipment, 751?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON

There were a lot of refugees in Germany, lots of them in Croatia. A lot of them were in the Netherlands and in Denmark, and so on and so forth. There was a ham radio operator from Bajina Basta who was used, so to speak. In other words, he was the one who enabled us to get in touch with the families in Germany, in the areas which were outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because ham radio operators from Tuzla could not contact other states.

utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, I would like to ask you a question with respect to the telephone system. utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: The telephone lines were cut off in the first part of July 2002. It was the Serb forces that did that on the radio relay knob near Tuzla. The -- Srebrenica is in such an area where the terrain configuration did not lend itself to a direct signal being transmitted from Srebrenica to Tuzla. There were certain radio relay knobs that had to amplify the signal, and that is why before the war in the vicinity of Tuzla on Mount Majevica there was a radio relay hub with an antenna installed. It received signals from the radio relay station in Srebrenica and forwarded the signal to Tuzla. These telephone lines were cut off in July 2002 [as interpreted]. And as for the second part of your question, you asked me whether there were any other systems in Srebrenica. In the PTT building there was an induction telephone switchboard which did allow access to a few people. And from then period on, in Srebrenica maybe five or six inductor telephone sets were installed in Srebrenica connecting, for the most part, the hospital. And then in the house of Dr. Nijaz Dzanic there were some of the hospital beds, and he treated the patients there as well. I believe that the organs of civilian authorities, if there were such organs in the municipality at the time, provided him with that sort of connection, in his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, did there come a -- I will rephrase the question. How long did you work, you and the other operators who operated the 745 and yourself, work on relaying messages to family members and did there come a time that you were no longer doing these duties, you yourself, but you had taken other -- taken up other duties with respect to operating the radio?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: As I've said, these activities involving the transmission of messages to the families in Tuzla or elsewhere lasted throughout June, July, and August of 1992, and only the messages were sent in this way. In September, October, November, and onwards, people realised that they could directly contact their family members in Tuzla and they wanted this. Therefore, afterwards people would come in, sit next to the radio equipment next to me or the Dautbasic brothers or whoever was operating the equipment; and, on the other side, in Tuzla, the family members would come to the radio club, to the radio operator, or sometimes the radio operator would call the refugee centre in Tuzla so that they could hear each other's voices via telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there. I would like to move to another subject matter. Did there come a time that you were aware of Muslim forces -- that Muslim forces had been organised in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: At that time the form of their organisation was not clear to me, the manner in which the Territorial Defence was organised, that was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say -- let me just interrupt you for a moment. When you say "at that time," could you give us a month and the year that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: When I say "at that time" I'm referring to 1992. Some forms of the organisation of the Territorial Defence became known to me only after the demilitarisation in 1993. I am not aware that in 1992 there was any kind of mobilisation carried out in any form; however, based on the events taking place it was clear that people started organising themselves in a way in order to defend their families. First of all, I would like to point out that there were many refugees who had arrived from the Bratunac municipality, from Glogova, from Voljevica. And wishing to return to their properties together with villagers from the Srebrenica area, they organised themselves in such a way as to deflect the Chetnik attacks. They did this all aiming to return to their homes. However, as time went by the attacks of Serb forces became much more intense and there were artillery attacks launched from Bratunac on Potocari, and people were forced to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to particular months in 1992 and ask you about your knowledge of the Muslim Territorial Defence at that particular time. In the months of May, June and July, were you aware of the Muslim forces and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In July of 1992, did you have a conversation with anyone regarding the formation or the organisation of Muslim forces in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not talk to anyone about the establishment of the Muslim forces in Srebrenica in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with a Hamid Alic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: In a certain sense, when it comes to organisation, I don't think that this involved, the organisation of military forces, no. What he mentioned to me was that within the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, there was a service called service for information, and it was headed by Hamid Alic. I was designated as person in charge of radio communication; by this I mean this piece of equipment, IC-751, which we used to establish contact and to relate information on refugees from Bratunac to the others in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stick to the question that was put to you, because I think you are somewhat answering at a tangent here. Let's go through it slowly. Earlier on in your testimony you told us how, in the early days, April, locals gathered around Naser Oric, around Hakija Meholjic, and Akif Ustic, and the following month, in May, around Zulfo Tursunovic in Suceska, Stari Grad, and Potocari, respectively. Did the situation remain always like that or did it change.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I mentioned people, persons that residents rallied around, that didn't mean that, for example, people who rallied around Naser Oric or somebody else remained there around them the whole time. Occasionally people would take 20p migrate, move from one area to another one. In that rallying, I saw no signs of organised resistance, no. This was done in an unorganised way. It just happened that people were there, and there was a need to defend themselves and they expressed a wish to defend themselves. But people could have also gone to other places. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did the situation remain like that , or did it develop into something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 I did not see that there was any higher form of organisation that would be more serious. Perhaps the reason for that was shortage of equipment and weaponry and all other elements that are needed in order for something to function properly. When it comes to communication means, it is clear to me nowadays - it was less clear to me in 1992 - that in order to equip a brigade, if applying proper standards, one needs really good communication equipment. And the equipment that existed in Srebrenica could not satisfy the needs of even a company, if I can say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Becirovic, but you haven't answered my question. My question, very simply put, was the following: The situation that you described to us earlier on, relating to April and May, where these people rallied in the way you explained, around these four persons, did the situation remain always like that, or did it develop into something else? You were about to tell us that in 1992 you were not aware of -- but then you again escaped and gave an answer which is completely unrelated to the question that I put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware that Hakija Meholjic, I think in May, left Srebrenica and went to the neighbouring villages with some of the people rallying around him. Because in Bratunac municipality, in the Skenderovici and Brezovica villages and perhaps in some other villages as well, the Serbs persecuted the inhabitants. So that in Osmace or Tokuljaci which were the villages populated by Muslims, he spent a certain period of time there attempting - at least that's how it seemed to me - to demonstrate that it was necessary for people to organise themselves. In those areas people organised themselves based on their village, place of location, because there was no sophisticated way of organising themselves. And these village organisations had to be united, had to be linked in a way. From April 1992 until demilitarisation in 1993, the situation in Srebrenica municipality was such that due to daily shellings, daily attacks, there was no possibility to create a more sophisticated kind of organisation which could coordinate the activities of smaller organisations in villages, therefore each individual in a village defended his own house. And towards late 1992, when the enemy offensive intensified, when the Chetnik offensive intensified, people started going further away from their villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was there anything -- have you ever heard of the Territorial Defence, Territorial Staff in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In 1993, after demilitarisation, I heard that a group of people attempted to organise the staff of the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica, which, in my view, did not have a very important role to play when it comes to organisations which existed in local communes. I think that certain people were named, appointed. However, I think that until November 1992, in Srebrenica, there was no one on the Staff to coordinate the Territorial Defence Staffs in local communes. The way they referred to these people was, they were Naser's people or they were Zulfo's people or they were people from Glogova or from Potocari; these were the terms used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, did there come a point in time, and specifically with respect to the months of June or July, that you gained knowledge about a meeting that had taken place involving the individuals you mentioned before, such as Akif Ustic, Zulfo Tursunovic, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And Hakija Meholjic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have mentioned that in the second half of July when talking informally to Hamid Alic, I heard that sometime in May there had been a meeting between Naser Oric, Zulfo Tursunovic, Akif Ustic, and perhaps Hakija Meholjic, and somebody else even, where they tried to organise the establishment of the Territorial Defence Staff; however, I know that following this, it didn't really materialise. And what I saw later, in terms of the conduct of the people, that certainly did not look like a proper organised take 20q establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you learn -- what, if anything, did you learn concerning Naser Oric at this meeting, that you were told?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Hamid told me that, in that meeting, Naser Oric was supposed to be the commander of the groups that assembled there and that other members were supposed to follow his orders; however, in reality that's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you a member, Mr. Becirovic, of the military -- had you been mobilised in Srebrenica in 1992 - well, let's take it specifically month by month. Between May and August, had you been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: If we picture a situation where somebody lined me up with other people and said, "Now you belong to this unit," no, that's not what happened. However, while I was in Suceska local commune, I saw that after the 1st of May, the Serbs started shelling that area intensely and frequently. And, together with other people from my village where I was born, I started standing guard, digging trenches, and I have to say that at the time I felt that it was an honour to be part of all of that. Once I arrived in Srebrenica, nobody told me, nor did I request to be become a member of any organised group. I performed the tasks that I have just described to you. And in my conversation with Hamid Alic, I learned that I was a member of the service for signals and informing, which was under the Presidency. I hope that you are satisfied with the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may be a problem with interpretation. I am going to read out to you what I have in English here in the transcript and then ask you a simple question to confirm whether I have the right thing or not. "I learned that I was a member of the service for signals and informing, which was under the Presidency." Is that what -- is this what you learned, or that you had been appointed as the person responsible for communications in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: When I say that I learned, that means that in my conversation with Hamid, I learned that. I didn't use the word "appointed," precisely because I was never informed of this in writing. There was no decision appointing me. I was simply told verbally that I am supposed to perform these tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, did you attend any of the meetings, the military meetings, where Zulfo Tursunovic, Naser Oric, Akif Ustic, or Hakija Meholjic was present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you describing these meetings as military meetings?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings with those individuals that I just named?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it clear, because I think I need to make this clear. The question that you need to answer is whether, on any occasion, you were present at a meeting where not all of them, Zulfo, Naser, Akif, and Hakija, but any of them were present, too. Any one of them was present, too. Meetings where you were present, happened to be present, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was never present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So when you testified earlier that orders were not followed, were you present when anyone refused to follow an order by Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have an objection for a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to stand up, Mr. Jones. Please rephrase your question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't spoken, as yet, at least on the part of the witness, on any orders that he knows of that had been given by Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, when you say -- said earlier on that, to your knowledge nothing was organised and orders were not even followed, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was in position to contact other people who were members of village guards, and based on my exchanges with them, I learned that the situation was as follows: For example, without the goodwill of Hakija Meholjic to go with his people to Potocari and help with the defence, this could not have happened. So if Hakija Meholjic or some of his people wanted to help in Potocari when the Serbs attacked, then he could have gone there; if they didn't want to go there, then why would they? I mean, nobody had a duty. Nobody had an obligation to go and help. This is why I'm saying that this was not an organised structure that could coordinate the activities of groups which existed in local communes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so that it is clear, you -- Hakija Meholjic did not actually -- did you have this conversation with Hakija Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we did not have any such conversation. I mention Hakija Meholjic by way of example. It could have easily been somebody else, Zulfo Tursunovic or Akif Ustic or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so that it is clear, you didn't have this conversation with Zulfo Tursunovic or anyone else in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this conversation is supposed to refer to. And the witness has been describing the environment and the situation as he perceived it and the inability of control. And so he hasn't said there was specific conversation in which this information was relayed to him; he is clearly relying on the much broader information base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know, I was inclined to intervene myself a moment ago along the same lines that you have followed, Mr. Jones, but I think it is -- the questions that are being put are legitimate. Because the witness initially said that he would speak to people and people would tell him this and that, and then he gave an example. And Ms. Richardson has asked him whether he got this information basically by any conversation that he might have had with Hakija Meholjic himself, and he said "no," categorically denied that. So now she is trying to see whether it would have been Zulfo Tursunovic, and then the following question, whether he ever had any such conversation with your client or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe the first question would be simply on what he bases that assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I mean -- but I won't -- I won't restrict Ms. Richardson in that respect. She can -- ask any question you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question was: Did you have this conversation with Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you have this conversation with Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: No, neither with Naser Oric or with Akif Ustic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to talk to you about Mr. Hamid Alic who you mentioned before. Could you tell us what position he held in Srebrenica during 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Before April 1992, he worked in Bratunac. He resided there. He was in charge of the telephone switchboard and the post in Bratunac. So the nature of his work, before the war, he was expelled from Bratunac. He survived execution. The nature of his work brought him to Srebrenica, and because he was involved in those tasks before the war, he found shelter in the building of the post office in Srebrenica. I really don't see any other reasons. He was familiar with the equipment, him and Naser Sulejmanovic slept in the post office building for a while. And it is my impression -- it was my impression at the time, during the first month of the war in 1992 that they were there in order to supervise the equipment and prevent the equipment from being stolen from the post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was he a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what -- I should ask. Did you attend any meetings -- did Srebrenica have a War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, during a certain period of time. I can't remember exactly when. All the information reached me subsequently, after the things happened. The War Presidency of Srebrenica was indeed established. I know that Hajrudin Avdic was appointed its president. As for some other members in 1992 and 1993, I didn't know any. This was not the subject of my interest for that matter. I know that people who were members of the War Presidency, of whom I learned subsequently, were not in Srebrenica at that time. Only Hajrudin Avdic was there, occasionally. And I also believe that the War Presidency did not function properly as it should have functioned in keeping with some provisions of the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you attend any of the meetings of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the month of July and your conversation with Hamed Alic, did there come a time that -- you said -- I will rephrase the question. What did you learn from Hamed Alic with -- regarding your duties in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: Hamed Alic only told me this: Since I was the one who had brought the IC-751 radio set to the post office building, I was in charge of this ham radio. I was to collect information on the people who had been expelled to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what, if any, contact did you have with Hamid Alic after this conversation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: We saw each other every day in the post office building. His office was very close to the room where I was with the equipment. He also told me at the time that he had been appointed the chief of communications services, and that I was a member of that service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like the witness to be shown an exhibit. This has not been tendered yet. So if the witness testifies from it, we can have an exhibit number assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be P532, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, could you take a look at that document that is before you. I would ask you to take a look at the names that are on that document and ask if you recognise any of the names and any of the people that are listed.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM BECIROVIC
utterances.text: I recognise the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let's start with the first name. Just for the record, this document, the title is "list of signal unit members staff" in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the first name that the witness is being referred to is the witness which appears on the first page of this two-page document and which bears ERN number 03592912. We're talking of Hasanovic, Hamdija, son of Mohamed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was asking the witness if he recognizes the name, the person and as you can see there is a duty attached. There is a duty column that lists him as a TG, ROTG, that's in English any way, radio telegraph operator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's simplify it, Ms. Richardson. Unless there is any particular question that you would like to put, may I suggest, Mr. Becirovic, look at these two pages and the second -- the first that I have already mentioned, and the second which has ERN number 03592913. check all of the details that there are on these two pages. Take your time. And then come back to us and tell us whether the information contained in it is correct, or whether you would like to correct anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I recognise all of these names. And my comment on the lists would be as follows: The first list which says the "list of signals unit members" and in brackets "staff", I know that these lads were members of the signals unit from demilitarisation onwards. I don't know why, in the last column here, it says "joined unit on" and the dates that I see here precede the demilitarisation. The second list is the list of signals unit members, in brackets, computer post. I know that Nedzad Ahmetovic [phoen], the person on under number 1, on this list, came to Srebrenica from Tuzla towards the end of March, 1993. He brought a lap top that he used in order to maintain communication with Tuzla. Senahid Mehmetovic [phoen] and Siridic [phoen] Hajrudin were the persons that Ahmetovic Nedzad educated to work on the computer. Now on to the third list, the list of the signals unit members, in brackets, post, which contains my name also, this is also a list of people who were members of the signals and information unit that was located in the post office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to close this chapter here, please close it. Otherwise we can adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's best we adjourn at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. So, Mr. Becirovic, are you going to have a rest now? We will -- tomorrow is in the morning as well? Yes. It's a morning sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow we will reconvene at 9 o'clock. I think it is in this same courtroom here, courtroom two. 9 o'clock. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, we have a very short issue to raise in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in preparing for the testimony of this witness, we received from our learned friends from the Prosecution a list with 110 exhibits, and this is equal to us not having received a list in the first place. None of the documents have been used so far. I believe that this behaviour of our colleagues from the Prosecution is not correct. It means a lot of work for us, because for each witness we prepare ourselves. We study all the documents and based on that we decide which documents to use ourselves. I would kindly ask our colleagues from the Prosecution to stop this practice which makes the work of the Defence team much more difficult. We would like to receive the exhibits that they really intend to use with the witness. Not even half of these documents will be used tomorrow. They would take seven days to at least -- to use only half of these documents let alone all of them. In any case, it is impossible for us to provide the list of our exhibits before we receive the list of exhibits that they are going to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson, if you want to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour, quite briefly. The proofing, matter of proofing is quite a lengthy one especially when you're dealing with a witness such as this. The exhibit list was provided and certainly it was my intention, at that time, to use most if not all of them. However I have revisited the exhibit list again last evening very late and I have decided not to use as many as I first proposed. Again, this goes hand in hand with the proofing process. And what I can do, in response to the Defence request, is give them an updated list of the ones that I will most likely use tomorrow. I think I have used some of the exhibits, but I definitely will not use all of the ones that I initially proposed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I do concede that the matter raised by Madam Vidovic does, indeed, involve or call for some more in-depth discussion on this practice. I mean, but I think for the time being we will restrict it to the, what is the bare essential. I mean they have done all of the work now, so at the end of the day the volume of work that this practice entailed with them, with us, with our staff -- I mean I had to decide whether to have all the documents selected or whether to have the four or five volumes that I have, which is what I opted for because otherwise my secretary would have stayed here almost the whole night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we need to be extremely careful here. I mean, we will not discuss it now. Please, if you can reduce this list to what you intend using, I think you will be helping the Defence. You will not be helping us, because at this point in time it would involve too much more work, but we don't have to prepare anything as such ourselves, or at least as near as much as the Defence has to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, that is not a problem. I can provide an updated list this evening, if not sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you require, we will discuss it further, but our message is definitely one which is -- should be loud and clear enough. There should not appear -- or the Defence should not be given enormous lists of all exhibits, from all the binders, when in actual fact then at the end of the day only a few or handful will be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour if I may respond so Your Honours are aware of how the proofing process has worked? When you're dealing with a witness such as this one where he has been proofed over a period of time and time is of the essence to provide the list, so as not to slow down the preparation process for the Defence, I provided a list that included all of the possible documents that I would use. And if I had, in fact, provided them the list when I revisited it, it would have been 12 o'clock in the evening, last night. So I apologise and Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Ms. Richardson -- Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do take note of what the court has said and it will certainly be improved upon in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure it will and I am sure you didn't do this in bad faith or anything like that. I'm not attributing anything like that to you, of course. But please do also realise that in your case, as a member of the team of the Prosecution, you're just have your Staff that will bring into the courtroom on a daily basis that trolley with all of the documents, they are always available there. The Defence can't keep them here and they have to bring the documents from wherever they keep them. They have to make the selection every evening or every other day, of the documents that need -- it takes a lot more work and preparation on the part of the Defence than on the part of the Prosecution. Please do keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand. What the Court has said and the Defence is duly noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And we will meet again tomorrow morning at 9 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Thursday the 21st day of April, 2005 at 9.00 a.m.
